transcript: In this site-specific production of Tartuffe, André De Shields makes a meal out of the titular con man. This Molière play from the 1600s is about how a complete fraud and swindler infiltrates a home under the guise of being pious and benevolent. The focus of this production seems to be on making it a singular theatrical experience. It takes place in the library of the House of The Redeemer on the Upper East Side, the cast is remarkably close to you wherever you sit, and really anything with André De Shields is an event. That said, on the whole it didn't totally click for me. The performances were fun but I felt the tone was uneven. It is a comedy, but it felt a little campy for my taste, and sometimes the campiness undercut what I gather is the point of the story — to show the insidious nature of hypocrisy and false piety, and to shine a light on how woefully easily we can be fooled. But the story is still interesting, and it's pretty obvious that this just exists as a star vehicle for André De Shields. He does not disappoint. He's probably among the oldest actors to ever play this role, but he has this majestic, almost larger-than-life presence and charisma that works well for this character and is exciting to witness in person. One word of advice if you plan to attend: For such an intimate space, the sightlines are kind of hit or miss because all the seating is uniformly on ground level. So if you're short, I’d get there early to secure a seat in the front. With that, another program for my collection.
